name: Mambwe-Lungu
confidence_why: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 10 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Bickmore, Lee. 2007. High-toned Mora Insertion Between Onsetless Morphemes in Cilungu. In Doris L. Payne & Jaime Peña (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 37th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 88-95. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Mambwe-Lungu is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's single title hit, Bickmore 2003 'The use of feet to account for binary tone spreading: evidence from Chilungu' (Frankfurter Afrikanistische Blätter 15: 23-47), is a tone paper (binary H-spread modelled with feet), not a word-stress statement; it is print-only: the journal's new OJS site (journals.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/fab) holds only Nr. 32 (2026) and returns no result for Bickmore, the Köppe title page is gone (publisher in transition), and Glottolog, Crossref, archive. HathiTrust/Google Books search-inside blocked). Newly downloaded and read: Bickmore's 2024 CV (bibliographic confirmation, saved) and Bickmore 1996 ROA-161 (Chilungu unbounded H-spread with word-final extraprosodicity; tone only). Everything read for this language -- Bickmore & Doyle 1995, Bickmore 1996, Rolle & Bickmore 2022 (privative /H/ vs toneless, mora TBU), Kagaya 1987, Siame 2019/2022, Lumwanga 2023, Bickmore 2007 TOC -- treats Cilungu/Mambwe as a mora-based H/toneless tone language with contrastive vowel length and phrase-penult spreading, and none states where word stress falls; the only 'accent' remark (Werner/Tucker 1940) is impressionistic and refers to prefix tone. No first-hand word-stress statement was read, so the best new statement is not found. Highest-value acquisition remains Bickmore 2007 Cilungu Phonology (537 pp., Harvard print / HathiTrust search-only), which is the place an explicit 'no stress / penultimate prominence' statement would appear; Bickmore 2003 is medium priority.

tone_statements.citation: Key, Michael & Lee Bickmore. 2014. Headed tone spans: Binarity and minimal overlap. Southern African Linguistics and Applied Language Studies 32(1): 35-53. doi:10.2989/16073614.2014.925218
tone_statements.quote: In many Bantu languages, there is a contrast between a sequence of level Hs (τ́τ́) and one of H followed by downstepped H (τ́!τ́). ... This can clearly be seen in an example from Chilungu (Key & Bickmore in prep.). (20) Chilungu fusion and downstep /tù-ngá-mù-lás-á/ → tùùngámú!lásá ‘we can hit him/her’ If two input Hs are immediately adjacent (/lás/ and /-á/), they surface as level H. If two input Hs are non-adjacent (/ngá-/ and /lás/), a downstep is observed between them, courtesy of rightward bounded spreading of the H on /ngá-/.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.1 'Fusion and downstep', ex. (20) (no printed pagination)
tone_statements.summary: OT (Headed Spans) paper; Chilungu data from Bickmore: H vs L, rightward binary H spread, adjacent Hs fuse but spread-derived adjacency gives downstep (n Hs -> n+1, sec. 4.2). No tone count; no stress.

tone_statements.quote: An acute accent indicates High tone, a grave accent indicates Low tone, and a raised exclamation point indicates downstep. The <+H> found in underlying representations indicates a “Melodic High” tone, defined below. [...] Since only High tones are “active” in Cilungu in the sense of having rules which insert, delete and spread them, I assume an underlying tonal contrast of H vs. Ø. Furthermore, I assume that the tone bearing unit in the language is the mora.

tone_statements.quote: Tones found in this study are as follows. For the level tones, there are a high tone (indicated as V́, V stands for a tone carrier unit), low (V, no mark) and ultra-low tone (V̀). In most cases, the ultra-low tone is found at the sentence-final position. The falling tones are found only in the sentence-final position. They are the falling tone from high level ([hook mark over V]), the falling tone from low level ([hook mark over V]) and the falling tone from ultra-low level ([hook mark over V]).

tone_statements.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei (1987). Tonal patterns of Cilungu imperatives. In Studies in Zambian languages. Tokyo: Institute for the Study of Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo Universit. pp. 473-478.
tone_statements.quote: These tonal patterns of the imperative vary with the verb types. There are two verb types found in Cilungu. One is verb type I which is defined as verbs in which the tonal pattern of the infinitive has no height change at any place in the word-medial position. The other is verb type II which is defined as having a height change from high to low immediately after the prefix (cf. Kagaya, 1987, "A Tonal Study of Cilungu Infinitive Verbs").

sources.note: Morphophonology (gliding, lengthening, harmony); no stress. Useful for its bibliography (Halemba 2007 grammar; Rupya/LMS 1962; Siame 2019).

sources.citation: Rolle, Nicholas & Lee Bickmore. 2022. Outward-sensitive phonologically-conditioned suppletive allomorphy vs. first-last tone harmony in Cilungu. Morphology 32. doi:10.1007/s11525-022-09391-3 (open access).
sources.note: Sec. 2.2 'Basics of tone system': 'Cilungu is classified as a privative tone system (Hyman, 2001), contrasting /H/ vs. O (toneless)'; TBU is the mora; unbounded H spread to the penult of the intonational phrase. No occurrence of 'stress', 'lengthening' or 'prominence' in the text seen (Springer HTML via direct download; PDF download blocked by bot challenge, text seen up to sec. 5.3).

sources.citation: Lumwanga, Chibwe Ronald. 2023. A comparative study of Bemba and Mambwe at phonological, morphological and lexical levels. PhD thesis, University of Zambia.
sources.note: Sec. 5.2 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 86ff.): tone shift and vowel length in Bemba vs Mambwe; stress/accent discussed only for English dialects in the literature review. Silent on Mambwe stress.

sources.citation: Siame, Pethias. 2022. A comparative analysis of phonological and morpho-syntactic variations in Lungu, Mambwe and Namwanga languages. PhD thesis, University of the Western Cape (hdl 10566/9982).
sources.note: Ch. 5 (pp. 111-125): suprasegmentals = tone (H/L, phonemic on short vowels, grammatical on long vowels) and vowel length (phonemic). No word-stress statement for Lungu or Mambwe (one loose use of 'stresses the syllables' about Namwanga reciprocals, p. 291).

sources.citation: Siame, Pethias. 2019. Towards writing a comprehensive grammar of the Mambwe language. MA dissertation, University of Zambia.
sources.note: Sec. 4.5 'Suprasegmental phonemes in Mambwe language' (pp. 49-51): only tone (H vs L, lexical and grammatical minimal pairs) and vowel length (contrastive; long before NC and after glides). Stress not mentioned for Mambwe.

sources.citation: Bickmore, Lee. 2014. Cilungu tone melodies: a descriptive and comparative study. Africana Linguistica 20: 39-62.
sources.note: Recent descriptive overview of Cilungu verbal prosody with a language-background section; open on Persee but blocked by altcha by automated download.

sources.citation: Bickmore, Lee S. (1996). Bantu tone spreading and displacement as alignment and minimal misalignment. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-161.
sources.quote: Such spreading can be seen clearly in the Chilungu verbal paradigms below, where an underlying H spreads rightward in an unbounded fashion, subject only to word-final extraprosodicity (cf. Bickmore & Doyle 1995).
sources.note: Uses Chilungu verbal paradigms (sec. 2.3, ex. 28) to illustrate unbounded rightward H-tone spread 'subject only to word-final extraprosodicity (cf. Bickmore & Doyle 1995)'. Tone only; nothing on stress in Chilungu (the word 'stress' occurs only for Idsardi's formalism and Hayes 1995 in the bibliography).

sources.citation: Bickmore, Lee S. & Michael T. Doyle. 1995. Lexical extraprosodicity in Chilungu. Studies in African Linguistics 24(2): 85-121.
sources.note: Nothing on stress: tonal analysis (prefix H, iterative rightward H spread up to the penult because the final TBU is extraprosodic); vowel length lexically contrastive plus compensatory lengthening 'in all positions except word-finally' (p. 90). 'Stress'/'accent' appear only as cross-linguistic analogies for lexical extraprosodicity.

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 1987. A Classified Vocabulary of the Lungu Language (Bantu Vocabulary Series 4). Tokyo: ILCAA. [pp. 1-6 'An outline of Cilungu']
sources.note: Outline sec. 1-3 'Tones and their Descriptions' (p. 5): tone carrier unit = V, N of NCV, Cw of CwV; tones H, L, ultra-low, and falling tones (the latter only sentence-finally); 1-4 syllable structure (all open). No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 1987. A tonal study of Cilungu nouns; A tonal study of Cilungu infinitives; Tonal patterns of Cilungu predicate verbs; Tonal patterns of Cilungu imperatives. In: Studies in Zambian Languages (Bantu Linguistics, ILCAA), pp. 269ff. Tokyo: ILCAA.
sources.note: Introduction (pp. 269-270) read: tone carrier units, H/L/ultra-low level tones, falling/rising tones only word- or sentence-finally; vowel before NC lengthened. Purely tonal description; no stress statement (image-only PDFs; intro pages read visually, remaining chapters are tone-pattern tables).
sources.venue: Studies in Zambian Languages (Bantu Linguistics, ILCAA)

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 1987. Rungu-go no meishi no akusento shiron / A tentative study of tonal pattern of the Ci-Lungu noun. Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA) 34: 1-34. [in Japanese]
sources.note: 'Accent' (akusento) in the Hattori-school sense = tonal pattern; analyses noun tone classes with high-to-low / low-to-high 'specification marks' by stem syllable count (tables pp. 31-34, discussion pp. 28-29). No statement about stress or a fixed prominence position.
sources.venue: Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA)

sources.citation: Werner, Alice (ed. A. N. Tucker). 1940. Mambwe Proverbs [with 'Phonetic and Grammatical Notes on Mambwe']. Bulletin of the School of Oriental Studies 10(2): 455-467. (scanned text from archive.org item dli.calcutta.05150)
sources.quote: Each vowel may be pronounced either long or short, accented or not, and sometimes they have what one might call an "even" accent. All syllables end in a vowel. ... The mu- of 1 and 3 differ very slightly in sound, rather in accent. No. 1 never takes an accent. Compare the native pronunciation of muntu and muti, and it will be seen that in the former both syllables are pronounced with the same stress and tone, in the latter there is a distinct accent on the mu.
sources.note: Impressionistic only: 'Each vowel may be pronounced either long or short, accented or not, and sometimes they have what one might call an "even" accent' (p. 459); 'Compare the native pronunciation of muntu and muti.. in the former both syllables are pronounced with the same stress and tone, in the latter there is a distinct accent on the mu' (p. 462, i.e. class-3 prefix tone). No positional stress rule.
sources.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental Studies

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 2: 名詞中にあらわれる音調は、平音調として高 (V́ にて示す。なお、V は音調単位)・中 (V; 無印)・低 (V̀) がみいだされた。また、文末環境に限り曲音調がみられた。これらの曲音調は、高からの下降調、中からの下降調および中からの上昇調である。 || p. 24: 今までみてきたように、この言語の基底形は音調そのものが各単位に指定されていると考えるよりも音調変化の位置が指定されていると考えた方がよい。 || p. 21: 基底形には、音節境界に位置する、高から低への変化を指定するマーク "┐" と、低から高への変化を指定するマーク "┘" があらかじめ指定されているものとする。[…] "┐" の前および "┘" の後の音調単位には自動的に高音調が割りあてられ、"┐" の後および "┘" の前の音調単位には自動的に低音調が割りあてられる。音調変化を指定するマークを持たない基底出現形の場合には、その全音調単位に低音調が自動的に割りあてられるものとする。 || p. 1 (English abstract): The tonal patterns of nouns were studied in the following contexts: (1) isolation, (2) aasí + ___ (It is not ___), (3) ___ + Adjective [...] both the basic representation and the derivation process are postulated tentatively. The other result of the study is that the tonal patterns depend on the noun classes. That is, nouns which consist of the prefix Ø- and ya(a)- show the different tonal pattern from that of other nouns.
sources.locator: p. 1 (English abstract), p. 2 (§1, tone inventory and tone-carrier units), p. 3 (downstep mark '!'), p. 21 (§3, underlying-form marks), p. 24 (§3-1-7, deciding…
sources.note: Confirms the catalog's 'tonal / lexical-tone' coding: nouns fall into lexically distinct tonal types (Ia, Ib, IIa-1, IIa-2, IIa-3, IIb-1.IIb-5, IIc, IIIa, IIIb, IV, V; Table 1 pp. 31-33) and the pattern is a property of the noun stem plus its class prefix. Refinements the catalog rule (empty) lacks: (i) three level pitches High, Mid (unmarked), Low observed in nouns, with contour tones (fall from high, fall from mid, rise from mid) only utterance-finally (p. 2); (ii) tone-carrier unit = CV, V, the N of NCV, the CW of CWV; NCV, CWV and CV1V2 syllables count as two units, word-final CVW as one

sources.citation: Bickmore, Lee Stephen (2007). Stem tone melodies in Cilungu. SOAS working papers in linguistics 15. pp. 7-18.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: First, as has been proposed for a number of Bantu languages, I assume that the underlying tonal distinction in Cilungu is one of High vs. ø i.e. Low tones are underspecified underlyingly, being introduced very late in the phonology by a rule of Default L Insertion. Second, I assume the TBU to be the mora. This is supported by the fact that Cilungu has a variety of different contour tones, all of which must be borne by a long vowel. Finally, Cilungu exhibits downstepped High tones, indicated by a raised exclamation mark. [...] Cilungu maintains a contrast in vowel length as well as tone in verb roots as seen below. [...] (4) a. lùk-á 'weave!' b. lúk-à 'vomit!' c. kòm-á 'cut!' d. kóm-à 'be strong!'

sources.quote: As for the level tones, there are high tone (indicated as v, V means a tone carrier unit here), low (V, no mark), and ultra-low (V) found in Lungu nouns. In addition, the falling tones and the rising tone are found only in either the word-final position or the sentence final position. [tone diacritics on the V symbols are lost in scanned] ... Tone carrier units of Lungu are V(vowel), N(nasal consonant) of NCV syllables and W of CW syllables.
